blocks.text: And when the flood had drowned the world in its waves, it rose above the Deucalionian waters.

This is also the position of most of the Scholastics on book 2 of the Sentences, Dist. 17; also of Tostatus and Cajetan on Genesis, of Bellarmine in the book On the Grace of the First Man, ch. 14, and of Malvenda, ch. 84 On Paradise. But we raise many objections to this view in a separate work, On the Earthly Paradise. From where, then, shall we say this olive leaf was brought? From Assyria, it seems, which in 2 Reg. XVII, 32. is said to be ארץ זית יצהר, or, as the Chaldee has it, ארע דויתהא עבדין משחא, a land whose olives make oil, that is, a land rich in olive trees, and very fruitful ones. For Noah's ark had come to rest on the mountains of Ararat, or of the Gordyaeans, which Assyria borders to the south. I would suppose that the dove, leaving the ark, flew off toward that quarter of the sky, drawn by the warmth of the south and also driven by the wind. For [II, 562] it is likely that the wind which God had raised to dry up the waters, Gen. VIII, 1., blew from the north toward the south. So in Ovid, at Deucalion's flood, Jupiter, appeased,
Scattered the clouds, and, the storm-clouds removed by the North Wind, showed the lands to the sky, and the heavens to the lands.
This dove, then, flying south into Assyria, could have plucked an olive leaf from some mountain, part of which the receding waters had laid bare.
